citeAs: Langlais, P.-C., Rosas Hinostroza, C., Nee, M., Arnett, C., Chizhov, P., Jones, E. K., Girard, I., Mach, D., Stasenko, A., & Yamshchikov, I. P. (2025). Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training. arXiv:2506.01732.
creator: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Arnett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov (PleIAs)
description: Common Corpus is the largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing approximately 2 trillion tokens of data that are either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses. It is multilingual, covering a wide variety of languages from main European languages to low-resource ones, and includes six collections: Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic. The dataset is designed to support fully open and auditable LLM pre-training while complying with data security regulations and AI legislation.
inLanguage: en, fr, de, es, la, it, pl, el, pt, ru, nl, da, sv, cs, sr, ar, zh, ja, and many others
name: Common Corpus
rai:dataBiases: The dataset acknowledges several biases: (1) English dominance — nearly 85% of Open Science documents are in English; (2) historical texts in Open Culture contain language reflecting outdated cultural norms around ethnic groups, women, and violence that do not meet modern ethical standards; (3) low-resource language coverage is still shallow despite multilingual efforts; (4) web data is a major source of harmful and biased content including sexual content, hate speech, and racial and gender biases. Toxicity filtering and PII removal were applied to mitigate these issues.
rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus is assembled from six collections: Open Government (financial, legal, and administrative data in the public domain), Open Culture (cultural heritage datasets including monographs and periodicals from over 13 languages), Open Science (scientific papers and documents from open archives and publishers), Open Code (code data from the Stack v1 and v2), Open Web (Wikipedia, Wikisource, YouTube Commons, StackExchange), and Open Semantic (Wikidata). Data was collected via APIs, large dumps (Collections As Data initiatives), and standard retrieval methods.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources include: SEC annual reports (Form 10-K, 1993–2024), WTO documents (1995–2024), AMF documents, EU procurement notices, GATT library documents (1946–1996), legal datasets (Caselaw Access Project, CourtListener, EUR-lex, Eurovoc, USPTO), digitized cultural heritage texts (books and newspapers from national libraries in France, US, Germany, Spain, Italy, Netherlands, etc.), scientific papers via OpenAlex and arXiv, code from the Stack v1 and v2, Wikipedia/Wikisource HTML dumps, YouTube CC-By audio transcripts, StackExchange Q&A, and Wikidata RDF triples.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Documents span from 1618 (Europeana Newspapers) to 2024, with the dataset itself first published in March 2024 and the current version released in February 2025.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web API, Web Scraping, Document analysis
rai:dataLimitations: Common Corpus does not collect the whole range of available open data (the "open data paradox"). Coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow. The 2 trillion tokens is suitable for pre-training models of limited size but larger models require significantly more data. The dataset does not contain data for instruction-tuning or specialized tasks, making it not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning. None of the curation methods can guarantee 100% accuracy (e.g., residual OCR errors, toxicity, PII).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Toxic content in public domain data is either removed or synthetically rewritten without the harmful language. OCR-corrected texts may be synthetically rewritten on highly deteriorated content. Wikidata RDF triples were translated into natural language sequences (e.g., "Q41309 | P:27 | Q171150" becoming "Franz Liszt country of citizenship Kingdom of Hungary"). A "refined" version for late training of about 1 trillion tokens was derived with more intensive, curation-based filtering.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing includes: (1) text segmentation using Segmentext model trained to handle broken/unstructured texts with digitization artifacts; (2) OCR error detection using OCRoscope (cld2-based 7-gram analysis) and OCRerrcr (DeBERTa-v2-style 400M parameter model); (3) OCR correction using OCRonos (Llama 3 8B-based model); (4) PII removal using Microsoft Presidio with custom regular expression patterns (replacing PII with fictitious but realistic values); (5) toxicity detection and filtering using Celadon (DeBERTa-v3-small, ~140M parameters, trained on 2M annotated samples); (6) for Open Code: removal of unwanted file types, license filtering, manual quality filters, removal of files with 75%+ digits, and line-ending normalization.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource with HuggingFace ensuring proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility. Ongoing data collection is planned as part of the LLMs4EU project, with plans to expand corpora in African languages (e.g., Swahili, Wolof, Bambara).
rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus enables open LLM research and development while complying with legal and regulatory requirements, including EU AI regulations. It supports open science as a shared research infrastructure. It contributes to the AI Commons and helps avoid the negative externalities of using copyrighted data. It enables development of multilingual models serving non-English-speaking communities. It was acknowledged as one of the main deliverables of the Paris AI Summit 2025 as the "largest open database to train Large Language Models."
rai:dataUseCases: Pre-training of large and small language models; multilingual LLM development; development of historical language models; training models for creative writing; developing vision-language models (VLMs) for document segmentation and processing; legal knowledge models; RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) models; creation of multimodal datasets, classifiers, synthetic datasets, and benchmarks.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext (custom text segmentation model); OCRoscope (cld2-based OCR quality detection tool); OCRerrcr (DeBERTa-v2-style 400M parameter OCR error detection model); OCRonos (Llama 3 8B-based OCR correction model); Microsoft Presidio (PII detection and replacement); Celadon (DeBERTa-v3-small ~140M parameter multilingual toxicity classifier trained on 2M annotated samples); fastText language identification model (for language distribution computation).
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: PII (Personally Identifiable Information) including phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses was identified and replaced with fictitious but realistic values using Microsoft Presidio. The paper notes that large open datasets contain staggering amounts of personal data, e.g., phone numbers in RedPajama, email addresses in S2ORC and peS2o, and IP addresses in the Stack.

null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol for missing values is described in the paper.

evidence.name: In this paper, we introduce Common Corpus1, the largest open dataset for language model pre-training.
evidence.description: The data assembled in Common Corpus are either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses and amount to about two trillion tokens. The dataset contains a wide variety of languages, ranging from the main European languages to low-resource ones rarely present in pre-training datasets; in addition, it includes a large portion of code data.
evidence.creator: Pierre-Carl Langlais Carlos Rosas Hinostroza Mattia Nee Catherine Arnett Pavel Chizhov Eliot Krzystof Jones Irène Girard David Mach Anastasia Stasenko Ivan P. Yamshchikov PleIAs, Paris, France
evidence.datePublished: The current version of Common Corpus, the one we describe in this paper, was released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit.
evidence.inLanguage: Common Corpus is multilingual (see Figure 1 and Table 2 for language coverage). Unlike many pretraining mixes, which are coposed mostly of English and code data, our dataset has strong representation for several languages, with the top nine languages constitute at least 10B tokens each.
evidence.citeAs: Pierre-Carl Langlais Carlos Rosas Hinostroza Mattia Nee Catherine Arnett Pavel Chizhov Eliot Krzystof Jones Irène Girard David Mach Anastasia Stasenko Ivan P. Yamshchikov PleIAs, Paris, France
evidence.isLiveDataset: Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset, with HuggingFace ensuring a proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus is available on HuggingFace as an aggregation of 10,000 parquet files and is composed of six collections: Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic. In total, the number of tokens in Common Corpus is 1,998,647,168,282.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: All other parts of Open Culture have been collected on a resource-by-resource basis using APIs and other standard retrieval methods whenever available. The largest extractions of this kind include Internet Archive (about 2 million monographs in multiple languages) and Delpher (50,000 Dutch monographs and periodicals filtered to match the Dutch copyright law for public domain).
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The code data we use comes from the Stack v1 and v2 (Kocetkov et al., 2023; Lozhkov et al., 2024). The Stack v1 contains 6.4TB of data and covers 30 programming languages, while the Stack v2 is approximately ten times bigger at 67.5TB and covers over 600 programming languages.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: A collection of various open datasets was first published under the name Common Corpus in March 2024. The current version of Common Corpus, the one we describe in this paper, was released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: To identify and replace PII, we use Microsoft's Presidio, an open-source state-of-the-art tool. With the base settings, Presidio identified on average 55-60% of texts that included phone numbers due to different possible number formats. By applying custom regular expression patterns that include most phone numbers, we increased this accuracy to 85%.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: We identify documents containing harmful language and either remove it or synthetically rewrite the document without the harmful language. With this approach, we aim to mitigate some of the potential biases and harms in the dataset, while still leveraging the high-quality and stylistically diverse data for high model performance.
evidence.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally Identifiable Information (PII), which is any information that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual's identity, is protected under legislation such as GDPR. Consequently, the new reguations put restrictions on LLM training data. In an analysis of large open datasets, there is a staggering amount of personal data in widely used datasets, e.g., large quantities of phone numbers in RedPajama, email addresses in S2ORC and peS2o, and IP addresses in the Stack (Elazar et al., 2024).
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Many texts there are historical periodicals and monographs from at least 80 years ago. Cultural norms surrounding the discussion of certain ethnic groups, women, and themes such as violence have changed dramatically. Many of these texts, therefore, do not meet modern ethical standards. Training models on these texts would lead to the reproduction and circulation of harmful language.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Common Corpus is far from collecting the whole range of available open data, which we call the open data paradox. In addition to this, even though the language diversity of the data is large, the coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow. Furthermore, the amount of collected data (2 trillion tokens) is suitable for pre-training of models of limited size, as in the Pleias model family. In addition, Common Corpus naturally does not contain data for instruction-tuning and any forms of specialized tasks.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Common Corpus aims to support the pre-training of fully open and auditable LLMs by making it legal to release the source even without the provision of fair use. It has been used to create a wider range of language model artifacts, including multimodal datasets, classifiers, synthetic datasets, and benchmarks.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus aims to support the pre-training of fully open and auditable LLMs by making it legal to release the source even without the provision of fair use. As defined by UNESCO, it is a shared research infrastructure that is needed to support open science and serve the needs of different communities.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We developed OCRonos model based on Llama 3 8B. OCRonos is versatile and supports the correction of OCR errors, wrong word cuts or merges, and overall broken text structures. We created a multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon, a DeBERTa-v3-small model (∼140M parameters), which we trained from scratch on 2M annotated samples.
evidence.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset, with HuggingFace ensuring a proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility.
